ANIMATED PREVIEW
THE PROJECT

What it is and why it exists

Ranks historical gold ground against where you actually find it, then reads USGS bare-earth LiDAR to pick out the creek beds and ravines themselves and score which one is the source. It overlays active claims and land status, lifts the terrain into a real 3D mesh, exports targets as GPX, and includes an in-page AI guide that points the map at its answer. Every data source is free public data.

Highlights

  • Ranks historical gold ground against where you actually find it — then reads USGS bare-earth LiDAR to pick out the creek beds and ravines themselves and score which one is your source.
  • Overlays active BLM claims, private property lines and public streams, and re-renders the terrain at every zoom so old diggings stay readable close in.
  • A 3D button lifts the map into a real elevation mesh you can tilt, spin and exaggerate — every overlay drapes onto the actual ground, so a bench or a creek bed reads as real relief instead of a flat outline.
HOW IT WORKS

The mechanism end to end

No hand-waving: this is the actual chain, in the order it runs.

01

Free data only

USGS historical production records, BLM claim and land-status services, and USGS bare-earth LiDAR — keyless endpoints, no data bill.

02

Read the terrain itself

The LiDAR bare-earth model exposes creek beds, benches and inside bends that a satellite image hides under tree cover, and the renderer re-drapes the terrain at every zoom so old diggings stay readable close in.

03

Score the ground

Each area gets a 0-100 score — roughly 75+ 'go check', 60-75 strong, 45-60 possible, under 45 weak — with walkable target zones.

04

Tell you if you may mine

Land-status overlays distinguish claimed land from BLM, National Forest, state and private ground, so the answer to 'can I dig here' comes before the drive.

05

Lift it into 3D

A real elevation mesh you can tilt, spin and exaggerate, with every overlay draped onto the actual ground.

06

Ask the guide

A local-model guide answers questions about the ground on screen and moves the map to what it is talking about.

BUILD IT YOURSELF

The steps in order, with the traps

This is the short version of what I would do again — including the parts that bit me first.

01

Prefer keyless public endpoints

No API key means no quota, no billing and no expiry surprise in a canyon.

02

Bound every remote call and mirror it

Public geospatial hosts flake — one host returned a 502 inside a 200 response. Keep a second host for the same dataset and a short timeout on the primary.

03

Never treat a 200 as data

Parse, and raise loudly when both sources fail — an empty list reads as 'nobody ever found gold here'.

04

Vendor the map library for the field

A CDN tag is a network dependency at open time, which is exactly the failure an offline map exists to survive.

05

Make the assistant read the screen

A guide answering from the last scan rather than the current view is worse than no guide.

WHAT I LEARNED

Notes from the build

NOTE 01Bare-earth LiDAR is the best free prospecting signal available — free data, real terrain.
NOTE 02Public data hosts go down quietly; bound the primary, keep a mirror, and fail loudly when both are gone.
NOTE 03An offline-capable map is a different engineering problem from a fast one.
